paragraphs: He advises them to cultivate a fondness for dress because, he asserts, a fondness for dress is natural to them. I cannot understand what either he or Rousseau means when they so often use this vague term. If they told us that in some earlier existence the soul was fond of dress and brought the inclination with it into a new body, I should listen with a half smile, as I often do when I hear someone hold forth about innate elegance. But if he meant only that the exercise of the faculties will produce this fondness, I deny it. It is not natural; like false ambition in men, it springs from a love of power.

Dr. Gregory goes much further: he actually recommends pretence, advising an innocent girl to belie her own feelings and not to dance with spirit, even when gaiety of heart would make her feet eloquent without making her movements immodest. In the name of truth and common sense, why should one woman not admit that she can take more exercise than another — in other words, that she has a sound constitution? And why, to dampen innocent liveliness, must she be darkly told that men will draw conclusions she little suspects? Let the libertine draw whatever inference he likes; but I hope that no sensible mother will check the natural frankness of youth by instilling such indecent warnings. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh; and one wiser than Solomon has said that the heart should be made clean, rather than that trivial ceremonies be observed — ceremonies that are not very hard to perform with scrupulous exactness while vice reigns in the heart.

Women ought to strive to purify their hearts; but how can they, when their uncultivated understandings leave them wholly dependent on their senses for occupation and amusement; when no noble pursuit lifts them above the petty vanities of the day, or enables them to curb the wild emotions that shake a reed at the mercy of every passing breeze? Is affectation needed to win the affections of a virtuous man?

Nature has given woman a weaker frame than man. But consider a wife who, by exercising her mind and body while discharging the duties of daughter, wife and mother, has allowed her constitution to keep its natural strength and her nerves a healthy tone: to ensure her husband’s affections, must she, I say, stoop to use art and feign a sickly delicacy in order to secure his affection? Weakness may arouse tenderness and flatter the arrogant pride of man; but the lordly caresses of a protector will not satisfy a noble mind that longs to be respected and deserves to be. Doting fondness is a poor substitute for friendship!

In a seraglio, I grant, all these arts are necessary; the epicure must have his palate tickled, or he will sink into apathy. But have women so little ambition that they are content with such a condition? Can they idly dream their lives away in the lap of pleasure or the languor of weariness, instead of asserting their claim to pursue rational pleasures and distinguishing themselves by practising the virtues that dignify mankind? Surely she has no immortal soul who can idle her life away, occupied solely in adorning her person so that she may amuse the listless hours and soften the cares of a fellow creature who is willing to be enlivened by her smiles and tricks once the serious business of life is over.

Moreover, the woman who strengthens her body and exercises her mind will, by managing her household and practising various virtues, become her husband’s friend, not his humble dependant; and if such solid qualities earn her his regard, she will not find it necessary to hide her affection, or to pretend to an unnatural coldness of constitution in order to arouse his passions. Indeed, if we look back at history, we shall find that the women who have distinguished themselves were neither the most beautiful nor the gentlest of their sex.

Nature — or, to speak with strict correctness, God — has made all things right; but man has sought out many inventions to spoil the work. I am referring now to the part of Dr. Gregory’s treatise in which he advises a wife never to let her husband know the extent of her sensibility or affection. A sensualist’s precaution, and as futile as it is absurd! Love, by its very nature, must be transitory. To look for a secret that would make it constant would be as wild a search as the hunt for the philosopher’s stone or the universal remedy; and the discovery would be just as useless, or rather harmful, to mankind. The most sacred bond of society is friendship. A shrewd satirist has well said “that rare as true love is, true friendship is still rarer.”
This is an obvious truth, and since its cause does not lie deep, even a slight inquiry will find it.

Love, the common passion, in which chance and sensation take the place of choice and reason, is felt to some degree by the mass of mankind; for there is no need at present to speak of the emotions that rise above love or sink below it. This passion, naturally heightened by suspense and obstacles, draws the mind out of its usual state and exalts the affections. But once the security of marriage lets the fever of love subside, a healthy temperature is thought insipid only by those who lack the intellect to put the calm tenderness of friendship and the confidence of respect in the place of blind admiration and the sensual emotions of fondness.

This is, and must be, the course of nature: friendship or indifference inevitably follows love. And this arrangement seems to harmonize perfectly with the system of government that prevails in the moral world. Passions spur us to action and open the mind; but once the object is gained and the satisfied mind rests in enjoyment, they sink into mere appetites, a personal and momentary gratification. The man who had some virtue while he was fighting for a crown often becomes a voluptuous tyrant once it adorns his brow; and when the lover is not lost in the husband, the dotard, a prey to childish whims and doting jealousies, neglects the serious duties of life, and the caresses that should build confidence in his children are lavished on the overgrown child, his wife.

To fulfil the duties of life, and to be able to pursue with vigour the various occupations that form the moral character, the master and mistress of a family ought not to go on loving each other with passion. I mean that they ought not to indulge those emotions that disturb the order of society and absorb thoughts which should be employed otherwise. The mind that has never been absorbed by a single object lacks vigour; but if it can remain so absorbed for long, it is weak.

A mistaken education, a narrow, uncultivated mind and many prejudices about sex tend to make women more constant than men; but for the present I shall not touch on this branch of the subject. I will go further still and put forward, without any thought of paradox, the claim that an unhappy marriage is often very beneficial to a family, and that the neglected wife is, in general, the best mother. And this would nearly always be the result if the female mind were more enlarged. For it seems to be the ordinary rule of Providence that whatever we gain in present enjoyment is deducted from that treasure of life, experience; and that while we are gathering the flowers of the day and revelling in pleasure, we cannot at the same time seize the solid fruit of toil and wisdom. The road lies before us, and we must turn right or left; whoever passes his life bounding from one pleasure to another must not complain if he gains neither wisdom nor a respectable character.

Suppose for a moment that the soul is not immortal and that man was created only for the present scene: I think we should then have reason to complain that love, that childish doting, ever grew insipid and lost its savour. Let us eat, drink and love, for tomorrow we die, would then indeed be the language of reason and the morality of life; and who but a fool would give up a reality for a fleeting shadow? But if, awed by observing the capacity of the mind for improvement, we scorn to confine our wishes or thoughts to so comparatively low a field of action, which appears grand and important only as it is connected with a boundless prospect and sublime hopes, what need is there for falsehood in conduct? And why must the sacred majesty of truth be violated to hold on to a deceptive good that undermines the very foundation of virtue? Why must the female mind be tainted with coquettish arts to gratify the sensualist, and to keep love from subsiding into friendship or compassionate tenderness, when there are no qualities on which friendship can be built? Let the honest heart show itself, and let REASON teach passion to submit to necessity; or let the dignified pursuit of virtue and knowledge raise the mind above those emotions which, when they are not kept within due bounds, embitter the cup of life rather than sweeten it.

I do not mean to refer to the romantic passion that accompanies genius. Who can clip its wings? But that grand passion, out of proportion to the puny enjoyments of life, is true only to the sentiment and feeds on itself. The passions celebrated for their durability have always been unhappy ones. They have gained strength from absence and from a melancholy temperament. Fancy has hovered around a form of beauty dimly seen — but familiarity might have turned admiration into disgust, or at least into indifference, and left the imagination free to start fresh game. On this view of things, Rousseau quite fittingly makes Eloisa, the mistress of his soul, love St. Preux when life was fading before her; but this is no proof that the passion is immortal.

Dr. Gregory’s advice about delicacy of sentiment is of the same kind: he advises a woman not to acquire it if she has made up her mind to marry. Yet this resolution, though perfectly consistent with his earlier advice, he calls INDELICATE, and he earnestly urges his daughters to hide it, even though it may govern their conduct — as if it were indelicate to have the ordinary appetites of human nature.

Noble morality! and consistent with the cautious prudence of a little soul that cannot see beyond the tiny portion of existence now before it. If all the faculties of a woman’s mind are to be cultivated only in so far as they concern her dependence on man; if, once she has obtained a husband, she has reached her goal and, basely proud, is content with so paltry a crown, then let her grovel contentedly, raised by her occupations scarcely above the animal kingdom. But if she is striving for the prize of her high calling, let her cultivate her understanding without stopping to consider what sort of character the husband she is destined to marry may have. Let her simply resolve, without being too anxious about present happiness, to acquire the qualities that ennoble a rational being; then a rough, unrefined husband may offend her taste without destroying her peace of mind. She will not shape her soul to suit her companion’s failings, but to bear them: his character may be a trial, but not an obstacle to virtue.

If Dr. Gregory meant his remark to apply only to romantic expectations of constant love and kindred feelings, he should have remembered that experience will banish what advice can never make us stop wishing for, when imagination is kept alive at the expense of reason.

I admit that it often happens that women who have nursed a romantic, unnatural delicacy of feeling waste their lives IMAGINING how happy they would have been with a husband who could love them with an ardent affection that grew every day and all day long. But they might as well pine married as single, and would not be one bit more unhappy with a bad husband than they are longing for a good one. That a proper education — or, to be more exact, a well-stocked mind — would enable a woman to bear a single life with dignity, I grant; but for her to avoid cultivating her taste in case her husband should occasionally offend it is to give up the substance for the shadow. To tell the truth, I do not see what use a cultivated taste is, if it does not make the individual more independent of the accidents of life; if it does not open new sources of enjoyment that depend only on the solitary workings of the mind. People of taste, married or single alike, will always be repelled by various things that do not touch less observant minds. The argument must not be allowed to turn on this conclusion; but, taking the whole sum of enjoyment into account, should taste be called a blessing?

The question is whether it brings more pain or more pleasure. The answer will settle whether Dr. Gregory’s advice is sound, and will show how absurd and tyrannical it is to lay down a system of slavery in this way, or to try to educate moral beings by any rules other than those derived from pure reason, which apply to the whole species.
